title: Ungrading Standing on One Foot
author: Susan D. Blum
summary: Susan Blum was given five minutes and one slide at a university workshop on alternative assessment and responds with the Rabbi Hillel story: the whole of ungrading on one foot is that humans are great learners but need authentic interest and the chance to learn from mistakes without punishment. She pushes back on the workshop's "small changes with big impacts" framing, saying a plug-and-play activity cannot transform education and that classroom structures, power relations, activities and feedback are intertwined. She describes shifting her role towards coach and her classroom from transaction to adventure, using portfolio conferences where students propose a grade with evidence. Her one concrete suggestion is reflection, in which students explain what they tried, what worked and what needs help, followed by revision. She argues this builds metacognition and confident, independent but interdependent learners, and a dentist-student anecdote shows why that confidence matters beyond school.
points: Ungrading boils down to authentic purpose plus safe, supported learning from mistakes; the mechanics are commentary.
Her view is that small, plug-and-play fixes cannot transform a course whose power relations and structures are intertwined.
A six-UnEssay sequence offers choice of genre, topic and audience, with drafts, workshops, reflection and peer appreciation.
Student reflection, followed by revision, is the one piece she would ask any instructor to try, partly because it is harder to outsource to AI.
The aim is judgment: students who can assess their own work, rather than asking whether it is what the boss wants.
quotes: Humans are great learners but learning requires authentic interest or need and the possibility of learning from mistakes without punishment, and with support.

In this not-AI-beautified slide I wanted to make the point that in ungraded classes there is mess and color and lack of linearity, not a simple pure cognitive-industrial one-size-fits-all solution to all problems.
Being a contrarian (I fundamentally dispute the idea that small changes can transform education, that a plug-and-play activity is transformative), I challenged the constraints I was given.
I’ve tried to transform the dominant atmosphere from transaction to adventure.

This is where students have an opportunity to explain what they were trying to accomplish, how they did it, what they did well, what might need work, what they might need help with. This contributes to that desired ability, metacognition, and it helps to promote what I consider one of the essential outcomes of education: confident, independent, but also interdependent learning.
In this moment of AI suspicion, reflection may be the only thing that students don’t panic about writing, especially if they’re graded on virtually everything else.
We have to help our students develop confidence in their own judgment of their work, rather than always having it externally provided.
Sages know the value of simplicity. We could do well to learn from them.
